method: Same-agent English/Marathi close reading and reverse paraphrase of the fixed-point equivalence, diagonal construction, self-printing analogy and lambda-combinator digression, with exact formula, macro, controlled-token, label and reference parity. No independent human or native-speaker review is claimed.
scope: Computability fixed-point theorem and equivalent formulations, self-referential program indices, and Curry/Turing fixed-point combinators.

samples.reverse_paraphrase: Write a name for φ_x(y) using the pair (x,y). No computable h can report whether every named computation halts: if it could, define partial g(x) to return zero when h says φ_x(x) is undefined, then choose its index e and obtain φ_e(e) defined exactly when it is not. This self-reference motivates a general fixed-point theorem rather than merely a contradiction. The two following formulations imply one another directly.
samples.checks: The temporary naming convention, h output cases, g diagonal cases, chosen index e, contradiction and two-way-equivalence explanation are preserved.

samples.reverse_paraphrase: For every partial computable binary g there is e with φ_e(y)≃g(e,y). Equivalently, for every computable unary f there is e with φ_e(y)≃φ_{f(e)}(y). From the first, set g(x,y)≃Un(f(x),y). From the second, use s-m-n to obtain f with φ_{f(x)}(y)≃g(x,y), then apply the fixed-point equality.
samples.checks: The universal quantifiers, partial versus total computability, e/y roles, both displayed formulas, implication directions and exact proof chains are retained.

samples.reverse_paraphrase: The theorem asserts the first fixed-point formulation. Construct computable diag(x) indexing the unary program y↦φ_x(x,y), using s(x,y)≃Un²(x,x,y) and s-m-n. Define l(x,y)≃g(diag(x),y), choose an index ⌜l⌝, and put e=diag(⌜l⌝). The five-step partial-equality chain yields φ_e(y)≃g(e,y).
samples.checks: The self-indexed first argument, arity of Un², primitive-recursive diag, l index, chosen e and all five aligned expressions remain exact.

samples.reverse_paraphrase: The analogy describes a string function diag that quotes and inserts its input at every literal x, letting print(diag('print(diag(x))')) print its own program. A variant print(x,y) repeats string x y times; the supplied getinput/print skeleton then prints itself y times. Replacing that skeleton with arbitrary g gives a program calling g on its own code and y. The source treats this as an intuition that readers should be able to reconstruct.
samples.checks: The exact verbatim code examples, C++/Java reference, quote substitution, repeated-output count and program-as-index interpretation are preserved.

samples.reverse_paraphrase: In lambda notation, diag(x)=xx and l(x)=g(diag(x)); setting k=ll yields k→gk and hence a fixed-point combinator. Curry's Y gives Yg and g(Yg) a common reduct; the later Turing Y directly reduces Yg to g(Yg), a stronger assertion.
samples.checks: The beta-equivalence versus direct-reduction distinction, both full Y terms, tagged lambda block and exact reduction arrows are retained.

source_observations: T335 records स्थिरबिंदू प्रमेय and स्वसंदर्भ as source-defined compounds under established index/computation vocabulary; T336 distinguishes Curry's common-reduct claim from Turing's direct reduction.
Code strings and verbatim programs remain in their original executable notation; they are examples rather than untranslated ordinary prose.
limitations: No independent human or native-speaker review has been performed.
Fixed-point and combinator compounds remain expert-reviewable.
